Republicans scramble to add third Trump nominee to the FCC

The tussle over the FCC's makeup comes amid a high-profile disputes with ABC and other media organizations and the looming change in control of Congress.

With just weeks remaining before Democrats take control of Congress, a scramble is underway to fortify the Federal Communications Commission with President Trump’s allies.

Trump in August nominated a third Republican — attorney Danielle Thumann Severs of North Carolina — to join the powerful panel for a five-year term.

Her nomination faces a critical test this week. Thumann Severs currently serves as senior legal advisor to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who has waged a nearly two-year campaign against prominent media organizations, including Walt Disney Co.’s ABC and Comcast’s NBC.

The Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation is scheduled to vote Wednesday on whether to send her nomination to the full Senate.

Hollywood Inc.

The agency’s chairman Brendan Carr said the commission will consider TV station mergers that exceed the current ownership limits on a “case by case” basis.

Democrats on the committee demanded Tuesday that the nomination process be slowed down.

Led by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington), the Democrats on the committee asked Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) to remove Thumann Severs’ nomination from consideration, suggesting that she was being teed up to help provide critical votes in support of “Carr’s controversial policies.”

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks,” the Democrats wrote in their letter this week to Cruz, who is wrapping up his tenure as chairman of the influential committee before Democrats take control in January.

The Democrats reminded Cruz that, in 2014, he wrote that controversial nominees “should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.”

FCC is taking a dim view of whether daytime and late-night shows on broadcast TV, such as “The View,” and “Jimmy Kimmel Live!,” deserve an exemption from the ‘equal time’ rules

Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), who also serves on the committee, separately challenged Thumann Severs’ candor when answering senators’ questions. Luján alleged that Thumann Severs “misled the committee and offered false testimony” during her confirmation hearing last week.
